title: Managed Identities
description: Discover how Azure managed identities eliminate the need to store credentials in your application code.

data.text: Developers often store database passwords, API keys, or certificate thumbprints in appsettings.json or environment variables. If someone steals that file, they have your credentials. Managed identities solve this by giving your Azure resource an identity Azure manages for you.
A managed identity is an automatically managed identity in Entra ID. You never create or rotate its credentials — Azure does it for you.

data.title: Types of Managed Identities
items: System-assigned — tied to a single Azure resource; deleted when the resource is deleted
User-assigned — standalone resource you can assign to multiple resources

data.caption: How a managed identity replaces secrets in application code.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A["App Service / VM / Function"] -->|"Request access token"| M["Managed Identity"]
    M -->|"No password needed"| E["Entra ID"]
    E -->|"Returns access token"| M
    M -->|"Returns token"| A
    A -->|"Call with token"| S["Azure Key Vault / SQL / Storage"]

data.title: Enable System-Assigned Managed Identity on an App Service
data.content: Turn on managed identity so your web app can authenticate to other Azure services.
data.code:
# Enable system-assigned managed identity
az webapp identity assign   --name myWebApp   --resource-group myResourceGroup

# Output shows the principalId you will use in role assignments

data.title: Get an Access Token from Code (C#)
data.content: Use the Azure SDK to request an access token for Key Vault without any secret in code.

data.text: A user-assigned managed identity is a standalone Azure resource with its own lifecycle. You create it once, attach it to one or more compute resources, and assign it roles. This is the right choice when several apps or slots need the same access, because the identity and its role assignments survive redeployments of the app.

data.title: Create, attach, and authorize a user-assigned identity
data.content: The identity must be attached to the app before it can request tokens, and it must be granted access to the target resource before the call succeeds.
data.code:
az identity create -g rg-shop -n id-shop-api

principalId=$(az identity show -g rg-shop -n id-shop-api --query principalId -o tsv)
identityId=$(az identity show -g rg-shop -n id-shop-api --query id -o tsv)

# Attach to the web app (this replaces existing user-assigned identities unless --identities is used)
az webapp identity assign -g rg-shop -n shop-api --identities "$identityId"

# Grant read access to Key Vault
kvId=$(az keyvault show -n shop-kv --query id -o tsv)
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$principalId" \
  --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "Key Vault Secrets User" --scope "$kvId"

data.text: Managed identity is not magic and it is not a secret in an environment variable. The compute host exposes a local token endpoint: the Instance Metadata Service at 169.254.169.254 on VMs and virtual machine scale sets, and the IDENTITY_ENDPOINT plus IDENTITY_HEADER pair on App Service, Functions, and Container Apps. The Azure SDK detects the environment, requests a token scoped to the target resource, and caches it in memory until shortly before expiry.

Because the endpoint is local and requires the host context, code running outside Azure cannot use it. That is why DefaultAzureCredential chains several sources: environment variables, workload identity, managed identity, and developer credentials such as the Azure CLI or Visual Studio. The chain lets the same code run locally and in production.

rows: Azure CLI or Visual Studio sign-in
App Service, Functions, Container Apps, VM

data.title: What interviewers look for
data.text: Be ready to contrast system-assigned and user-assigned identities, and to explain that the identity needs both a role assignment on the target and code that requests a token for the right scope. "It removes secrets, not authorization" is the key insight.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Managed identities remove secrets from code entirely.
System-assigned identities live and die with the Azure resource.
User-assigned identities are reusable across multiple resources.
DefaultAzureCredential automatically picks up the managed identity in Azure.
data.takeaway: Always use managed identities when running inside Azure. They are more secure than any client secret.
